title: Fallout warning: what to do first
summary: Get inside the nearest building now and go to the basement or the middle of it, away from the walls and roof. Stay in for at least 24 hours unless an immediate danger such as a fire, gas leak, collapse or serious injury forces you out. Don’t drive or walk away through fallout, and don’t go out to get family.
doFirst: Warning or flash? Get inside the nearest building now and move away from windows (Ready.gov). Caught outside when it goes off: lie face down to protect bare skin from the heat and flying debris, then get inside as soon as the shockwave has passed (Ready.gov).

Go to the basement or the middle of the building, as far from the walls and roof as you can (CDC). Brick or concrete buildings and basements are best, but being inside any building is better than being outside (CDC).

Stay inside for at least 24 hours (Ready.gov, CDC). Leave only if an immediate danger such as a fire, gas leak, building collapse or serious injury forces you out, or officials tell you to (Ready.gov). Don’t go out to get family: stay where you are (CDC).
Came in from outside? Carefully take off your outer layer of clothes and put them in a bag, then wash or wipe the skin and hair that were uncovered (Ready.gov, CDC).
Close windows and doors. Turn off fans, air conditioners and forced-air heating that bring in outside air (CDC). Listen to a battery or hand-crank radio (Ready.gov).

list: If you are warned that a radiation hazard is possible, get inside the nearest building at once and move away from windows (Ready.gov).
Put as many walls as you can between you and the outside (Ready.gov).
For a nuclear explosion, if you have warning, take cover from the blast behind anything that might give protection (Ready.gov).

sections.h: At the flash and the blast

list: Outside: lie face down to protect bare skin from the heat and flying debris (Ready.gov).
After the shockwave passes, go inside the nearest building as quickly as you can (Ready.gov).
If you must be outside and can’t get inside right away, cover your mouth and nose with a mask, cloth or towel (CDC).

blocks.p: A nuclear explosion on the ground can suck material up into the air and drops it back as dangerous, sand-like radioactive particles called fallout (Ready.gov).

blocks.warn: After a detonation you will have 10 minutes or more to find a good shelter before fallout arrives (Ready.gov, FEMA planning guidance). Use those minutes to get inside. Being out in fallout that is falling or has just fallen may be fatal (NYC Health).

blocks.p: If a multi-story building or a basement can be reached within a few minutes of the explosion, go there at once (Ready.gov). Brick or concrete buildings are best, and underground parking garages and subways can also give good shelter (Ready.gov).

list: Don’t try to drive or walk out of the area. Cars and other vehicles are not adequate shelters (FEMA planning guidance). FEMA strongly discourages people leaving on their own, and says that, unless a fire or other immediate danger forces you, no evacuation should be tried until there is basic information about where the fallout fell (FEMA planning guidance).
Don’t go out to get loved ones. Going outside to get them could expose you and them to dangerous levels of radiation (CDC). Don’t pick up children from school or daycare (NYC Health).
Let people in. Giving shelter to someone who was outside can save their life (CDC). They take off their outer layer of clothes before they come in, if they can (CDC).

blocks.p: Stay inside for at least 24 hours, and then until officials tell you to leave. How long, what changes it, and what to do if no one ever says, are in How long to stay in.

list: Follow instructions from emergency officials (Ready.gov). Listen to local radio for the radiation hazard where you are (FEMA planning guidance).
A battery-powered or hand-crank radio keeps working when other ways of getting news fail (Ready.gov).
No one broadcasting? Keep sheltering. FEMA’s planning guidance: with no information at all, sheltering still protects against fallout radiation.

blocks.p: Close windows and doors, and turn off fans and heating that pull in outside air. Never burn anything in a sealed room. How to keep a closed-up house liveable, including heat in winter, is in Living in a closed-up house.

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

blocks.p: If you are sick or injured, listen for instructions on how and where to get medical care (Ready.gov). First aid is in Emergency.

blocks.label: Potassium iodide (KI): what it can and can’t do

blocks.p: These topics cover fallout from a nuclear explosion. A nuclear power plant accident has its own official plans and is not covered in this app yet.
